extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of 18th-century political/social essays; readers of the British Repository and general public interested in politics, law, theatre, and agriculture
extracted.subtask_description: A set of 18th-century essays and letters addressing censorship, the stage and press, agricultural policy, customary practices, and criminal-law theory; mixes literary criticism, political philosophy, and practical policy argument. Useful for understanding contemporary standards and arguments about liberty, punishment, theatre, and economic policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary privilege for speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions in parliament ought only to be examined and punished there (i.e., words spoken in the House should be judged by Parliament, not by external courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page discusses the attorney-general's prosecution (Anno 1628) of three Commons members and the plea that parliamentary speech should be judged only within Parliament; contrasts this principle with prosecutions and punishments (e.g., Sir John Eliot fined and imprisoned) as an anti-pattern showing danger when external courts punish parliamentary speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech as foundation of a free constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A free constitution and freedom of speech have reciprocal dependence and cannot subsist without each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that suppressing inquiry and speech is effective policy for arbitrary governments but destructive for free societies: suppression breeds smothered resentment that can discharge in violence. Examples: Star Chamber prosecutions, silencing of critics, and later popular backlash. Implicit guidance: protect free expression to preserve constitutional liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treason requires an overt act; unpublished thoughts/writings are not treason
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing that remains private and unpublished is a covert fact and cannot constitute the overt act necessary for a treason conviction; 'scribere et publicare est agere' (to write and publish is to act) — mere imagining is not an immediately punishable treason without an overt act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sidney trial is used as the central example: his defence that his manuscript (never published or imparted) could not be an overt act within treason statutes is recounted; judge Jefferies' rejection and the packed jury are presented as a legal abuse. Anti-pattern: construing private speculations or 'known principles' as sufficient proof of treason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of punishing words by remote inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge may illegitimately construe innocent expressions into capital crimes by remote inferences and innuendoes, producing little security for citizens' lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney's execution is cited as a 'pregnant instance' of why laws punishing words are dangerous. Guidance: law and judges should not permit distant innuendoes to convert general political speculation into criminal intent; respect for reasoned defence and evidentiary overt acts is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary standard for the stage and press (comedy and satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy and satire should promote amiable, rational, manly characters and point resentment against vice rather than attack virtue, religion, or public spirit; satire should emulate Horace, Juvenal, and Boileau in targeting vice with generous resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes licenser-managed theatre that encouraged immodesty, double entendre, lewd representation, and the ridicule of religion and public spirit. Positive example: Steele and Addison rescued the stage by recommending amiable, rational characters, displacing bawdy and debauched portrayals. Anti-patterns: stage and press used as battering engines against religion, virtue, and liberty; ridicule of citizens (e.g., aldermen depicted as sneaking hypocrites) is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to using censorship and corporal punishment to suppress dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Using prosecutions, fines, mutilation, and perpetual imprisonment for writers and critics is an instrument of intimidation that suppresses public debate and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Prynn, Burton, and Bastwick fined, mutilated and imprisoned for writing on church government; such punishments are described as binding down gentlemen into servile fear and preventing public defence of liberties. Guidance: avoid corporal/infamous punishments for political or theological dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy consistency in trade/export restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the principle is to prohibit exportation to make goods cheaper domestically, that policy must be applied consistently and carried through — partial, inconsistent application produces perverse outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The farmer's letter argues that prohibiting wool export to favor domestic manufacturers while allowing exports of finished cloth keeps prices up and harms farmers; the counsel is 'when you are sure you have a good principle, stick to it and carry it through.' Anti-pattern: selective restrictions that benefit intermediaries but hurt primary producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair compensation/indemnity when public measures harm private parties
rubrics_metrics.description: When government takes measures (even for public good) that legally or effectively deprive private parties of expected gains, those parties should be indemnified from the public treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The farmer pleads that if export prohibition is necessary and right (yet contrary to law), and indemnity is to be passed for ministers, then indemnity should also be provided to those (farmers) injured by the policy. Example: farmers losing a guinea a quarter due to export ban — public compensation recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-welfare principle: avoid creating dependence; encourage self-provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Public provisions for the poor can reduce incentives for self-help and industry; better to lead or drive the poor out of poverty than make them easy in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist observes in other countries that greater public provisions correspond with more idleness, drunkenness, and insolence among the poor; recommends repeal of some poor laws and reliance on private charities and industry to foster frugality and sobriety. Implicit policy guidance: design poor relief to incentivize labour and self-reliance rather than create dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishments (punishment should fit the offence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments should be proportioned to the offence; imposing death for relatively minor thefts (e.g., gauze worth fourteen shillings threepence) is unjust and tantamount to murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts Mosaic law's fourfold restitution with contemporary capital punishments and criticizes cases at the Old Bailey; argues against using the pretext of 'preventing crimes' to justify excessive punishments. The French pamphlet advocating proportionate punishments is cited approvingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle favoring erring to prevent wrongful punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better that many guilty persons escape than that one innocent person suffer — a longstanding maxim of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim is presented as generally approved and used to critique sanguinary proposals for universal capital punishment; serves as a constraint on severity of penal statutes and on judges' readiness to inflict ultimate punishments.
